app.title: SondeHub V2 — Live radiosonde tracking
app.description: Live tracking of weather radiosondes: flight paths, landing predictions, receivers.
app.about.subtitle: Live tracking of weather radiosondes
app.about.intro1: Every day, more than 1,500 radiosondes are launched around the world beneath weather balloons. They measure temperature, humidity and wind up to more than 30 km altitude, then descend by parachute once the balloon bursts.
app.about.intro2: A network of radio amateurs decodes their signals and shares them via SondeHub. This interface shows that data live, along with landing predictions to help recover them.
app.about.faq.heading: Frequently asked questions
app.about.faq.whatA: A small electronic package weighing a few hundred grams, carried aloft by a balloon filled with helium or hydrogen. It measures pressure, temperature and humidity, derives the wind from its GPS, and transmits everything by radio every second. Weather services launch them about twice a day (around 00:00 and 12:00 UTC) to feed forecasts. At around 30 km altitude the balloon bursts and the sonde descends under a small parachute.
app.about.faq.dataQ: Where does the data come from?
app.about.faq.dataA: Radio amateurs and enthusiasts, often with very simple receiving equipment (an SDR dongle and an antenna), decode the signals and upload them to the SondeHub network, which makes them freely available. Predicted flight paths and landing points are calculated by the Tawhiri model (CUSF) from wind forecasts. SondeHub V2 only displays this data.
app.about.faq.accuracyQ: How accurate is the landing prediction?
app.about.faq.accuracyA: It depends mainly on the quality of the wind forecasts. Rough during the ascent, it becomes much more precise during the descent as the sonde gets closer to the ground: it is usually accurate to within a few kilometres. The sonde often drops below the radio horizon before touching down, so the last received position remains a valuable clue.
app.about.faq.foundQ: I’ve found a sonde — what should I do?
app.about.faq.foundA: It is harmless. You can keep it, or recycle it (electronics and batteries) according to your local rules. Please report it on SondeHub using the ‘Report recovery’ button on its panel: this helps the whole community. For your safety, respect private property, take care near roads, and never climb a tree or go near a power line to retrieve it.
app.about.faq.alertsA: Enable your location, then landing alerts in the layers panel (to the right of the map). SondeHub V2 will notify you when a landing is predicted near you, as long as the page stays open.
app.about.legend.heading: Legend
app.about.shortcuts.heading: Shortcuts
app.about.credits: Data: SondeHub (Project Horus) — public API api.v2.sondehub.org. Predictions: Tawhiri (CUSF). Basemaps: OpenFreeMap, OpenStreetMap, Esri, OpenTopoMap. Independent project, not affiliated with SondeHub. If you recover a sonde, please report it on sondehub.org.
app.help.burst.title: Burst
app.help.burst.text: As it rises, the balloon expands as the pressure drops until it bursts, usually between 20 and 35 km altitude. The sonde then descends under a small parachute.
app.help.maxAlt.title: Max altitude
app.help.maxAlt.text: Highest point reached so far. During the ascent, the predicted burst altitude is shown below it.
app.help.prediction.title: Prediction
app.help.prediction.text: Flight path and landing point calculated by the Tawhiri model from wind forecasts, then recalculated as the flight progresses. The uncertainty is typically a few kilometres and decreases as the sonde nears the ground.
app.help.landing.title: Predicted landing
app.help.landing.text: Point where the sonde is expected to reach the ground, calculated by the Tawhiri model from wind forecasts and updated as the flight progresses. Allow for a few kilometres of uncertainty.
app.help.lost.title: Signal lost
app.help.lost.text: The sonde is no longer heard by any receiver. Most often it has simply dropped below the stations’ radio horizon during descent and kept falling: it is then probably close to the estimated landing point.
app.help.rate.title: Ascent / descent rate
app.help.rate.text: Average vertical speed of the flight, used for the prediction. A balloon typically ascends at 4–6 m/s; under its parachute, the sonde falls fast at altitude, then slows to around 5 m/s near the ground, where the air is denser.
app.help.vspeed.title: Vertical speed
app.help.vspeed.text: Rate at which the sonde is rising (+) or falling (−). The balloon ascends at around 5 m/s; just after burst, the sonde falls very fast in the thin air, then slows under its parachute as it nears the ground.
app.help.hspeed.title: Horizontal speed
app.help.hspeed.text: Speed over the ground, driven by the wind. It often peaks at around 10 to 12 km altitude, in the jet stream. It is calculated from successive GPS positions.
app.help.trajectory.title: Flight path
app.help.trajectory.text: Path followed by the sonde since launch, seen from above (north up) or in profile (altitude against distance travelled). The dotted line shows the predicted remainder up to landing.
app.help.sensors.title: Sensors & telemetry
app.help.sensors.text: Measurements transmitted by radio from the sonde: air temperature, humidity and pressure (the weather ‘sounding’ that feeds forecasts), plus technical data (battery, GPS satellites, frame number).
app.help.profile.title: T / RH sounding
app.help.profile.text: Temperature and relative humidity profile measured during the ascent, against altitude. This is the weather data the sonde is there to collect.
app.help.snr.title: SNR
app.help.snr.text: Signal-to-noise ratio (in dB) measured by the receiver: the higher it is, the better the reception. Below ~6 dB, decoding becomes difficult.
app.help.elevation.title: Elevation
app.help.elevation.text: Angle of the sonde above your horizon (0° = horizon, 90° = directly overhead). When negative, it is below the horizon and out of direct radio range.
app.help.receivers.title: Receivers
app.help.receivers.text: Stations run by radio amateurs and enthusiasts that receive and decode the sonde’s signal (around 400 MHz) and share its positions on SondeHub. Car icons are mobile receivers.
app.welcome.title: Welcome to SondeHub V2

sidebar.tech.title: Technical details
sidebar.guide.title: The flight of a radiosonde
sidebar.guide.intro: Every day, weather stations launch balloons carrying a small sonde. On the way up it measures temperature, humidity and wind, and transmits its data by radio. These measurements feed weather forecasts all over the world.
sidebar.guide.ascentText: The balloon rises at about 5 m/s (18 km/h) for 1 h 30 min to 2 h.
sidebar.guide.burstText: At around 20 to 35 km altitude, the balloon, now enormous, bursts.
sidebar.guide.descentText: The sonde comes back down under a small parachute in 30 to 45 min.
sidebar.guide.landedText: It often lands several tens of kilometres from the launch site. You can go looking for it and report your find.
sidebar.guide.lost: Signal lost: the sonde is no longer being received, usually because it has dropped too low for the antennas. By then it is often already on the ground.

sonde.evolution.title: Prediction history
sonde.atmo.skewTHelpText: The meteorologists’ diagram: pressure (and therefore altitude) increases upwards, and the isotherms are skewed at 45°. Where the temperature (black) and dew point (blue) lines come together, the air is close to saturation: cloud is likely. The surface parcel (dotted) shows how a lifted bubble of air cools: when it lies to the right of the temperature curve, it is warmer than its surroundings and rises on its own (instability, possible thunderstorms).
sonde.atmo.skewTPending: The Skew-T will appear once the sonde has transmitted enough measurements during its ascent (a profile of at least 2 km).
sonde.atmo.windHelpText: The sonde has no anemometer: it drifts with the air. The wind in each 250 m layer is derived from its GPS movement during the ascent, which smooths out the swinging beneath the balloon.
sonde.atmo.purpose: What is it for? These temperature, humidity and wind profiles feed numerical weather prediction models. Nearly 900 stations around the world launch a balloon every day, usually at around 00:00 and 12:00 UTC.

sonde.view3d.title: 3D view
sonde.view3d.helpText: The column represents the air above the area the sonde has flown over. Its walls show the layers of the atmosphere: the troposphere, where clouds and weather form, then the drier, calmer stratosphere. The tropopause separating them is the one measured by this sonde when it crossed it, or otherwise a typical value for the latitude. The pale bands mark clouds the sonde passed through (humidity above 90 %).

charts.wind.hodographNote: Each dot is the tip of the wind vector (where it blows towards) at one altitude, smoothed over 1 km, with rings in {unit}. A curve that turns clockwise with height indicates a wind that veers with altitude, typical of warm advection.
charts.indices.title: Indices
charts.indices.help: CAPE: energy available to a bubble of air lifted from the surface (J/kg); CIN: energy that must be overcome to set it off. LI: temperature difference at 500 hPa between the environment and the bubble, negative if the bubble is warmer. K and Total Totals combine temperatures and humidity at 850, 700 and 500 hPa. LCL: level at which the bubble condenses, the base of cumulus clouds. Shear: difference in wind between the surface and 6 km; above 70 km/h it favours organised thunderstorms.
charts.indices.pressureComputed: This sonde does not measure pressure: it is derived from GPS altitude and temperature (typical error of 1 to 2 %).
charts.indices.surfaceParcelNote: Surface parcel: median of the lowest 50 hPa.

lib.insights.cold.text: It was {start} at launch and {coldest} at around {altitude}: on the way up, the air cooled by about {lapse}, because it expands as the pressure drops.
lib.insights.tropopause.title: Tropopause at around {altitude}
lib.insights.tropopause.text: Above this, the temperature stops falling ({temperature} at this level). It is the boundary between the troposphere, where clouds and weather form, and the drier, calmer stratosphere.
lib.insights.jet.title: Jet stream
lib.insights.jet.text: {speed} at around {altitude}: this is the jet stream, a corridor of very fast wind that circles the planet and carries balloons tens of kilometres away.
lib.insights.wind.title: Strongest wind
lib.insights.wind.text: {speed} at around {altitude}. It is this upper-level wind that carries the balloon far from its starting point.
lib.insights.cloud.title: Probable cloud
lib.insights.cloud.text: Between {from} and {to}, humidity exceeded 90 %: the sonde probably passed through a cloud.
lib.insights.clouds.title: Probable cloud layers
lib.insights.clouds.text: Between {from1} and {to1}, then between {from2} and {to2}, humidity exceeded 90 %: the sonde probably passed through clouds.
lib.insights.dry.title: Fairly dry air
lib.insights.dry.text: Humidity never reached 90 % below 12 km: probably no thick cloud along its path.
lib.insights.pressure.textBurst: At this altitude, the air pressure is only about {pressure} hPa, {ratio} times lower than at ground level. The balloon expands as the air thins, until it bursts.
lib.insights.pressure.textAscending: At this altitude, the air pressure is only about {pressure} hPa, {ratio} times lower than at ground level. The balloon expands as the air thins and will eventually burst, usually between 20 and 35 km.
lib.insights.pressure.textLastSignal: At this altitude, the air pressure is only about {pressure} hPa, {ratio} times lower than at ground level. The balloon expands as the air thins until it bursts, probably shortly after this last signal.

atmo3d.track.solidDark: Solid line: the path already travelled. Its colour shows the altitude at each point, from dark blue near the ground to very light blue at high altitude.
atmo3d.track.solidLight: Solid line: the path already travelled. Its colour shows the altitude at each point, from light blue near the ground to midnight blue at high altitude.

atmo3d.track.prediction: Pink dashes: the predicted path to landing, recalculated every minute.
atmo3d.track.reverse: Grey dots: the estimated launch path, before stations started receiving the sonde.
